newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel meeting on market reform to resume later.
newsitem.headline: Israel meeting on market reform to resume later.

text.p: The Israeli cabinet will resume on Sunday evening a meeting to discuss a package of reform measures for Israel's capital market, Treasury Director-General David Brodett said.
Debate on the reforms began on Sunday morning but the meeting has adjourned until 1600 GMT.

A tax on savings of less than 10 years is by far the most controversial of the measures recommended by a panel headed by Brodett that aim to increase long-term savings. The committee was formed in the wake of a collapse in bond prices in July.
At a press briefing following the morning meeting Brodett said that no one had an alternative that could achieve the goal of revitalising the capital market.

He said the tax on short- and medium-term savings was meant to finance special tax benefits for pension fund savings. The tax changes will improve the distribution of income in Israel as the savings tax is a tax on the rich, he added.
During the meeting opposition to the tax was voiced by both Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel and Avigdor Lieberman, director general of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office.
Economics Professor Amir Barnea, a member of the Brodett committee, said he could not see any compromise that would involve giving up the recommendation to tax short-term savings.
"This was at the heart of our report," he said. The report has the backing of Finance Minister Dan Meridor.

The other Brodett recommendations are not expected to encounter strong opposition. These include measures that would restrict sales of special high-yield government bonds to pension funds and reduce the tax rate on dividends.
